idiom_name: one namespace per module (folders mirrored), internal as the assembly-wide private, project/assembly for a hard boundary
implementation_notes: A C# module is a namespace matching the folder path (file-scoped namespace syntax in C# 10 or later), with the published surface marked public and everything else left internal or file-scoped. Namespaces are implicitly public and cannot carry access modifiers, so the only compiler-enforced boundary they give is the file modifier and convention; the enforceable unit is the assembly, where internal members are visible only inside the declaring assembly. A module that needs a hard boundary therefore becomes its own project - its public API is what other assemblies may use, with InternalsVisibleTo for test or friend assemblies. Most .NET domain code uses namespace plus internal as the module and keeps public deliberately small.
pitfalls: Namespaces provide no encapsulation: any assembly can write using Acme.Billing; and reach every public type - internal or file access is what actually hides something.
Defaulting to public makes every later change a breaking change; default to internal and widen only when another assembly needs the type, since widening is compatible and narrowing is not.
One assembly can contain several namespaces and one namespace can span assemblies, so 'the module' stays ambiguous unless you decide whether the assembly or the namespace is the unit.
Namespace names mirror folders and the root namespace follows the project, so promoting a namespace to its own project renames it; settle the project/namespace split before publishing packages.
